findings.paper_title: Annual Governance Statement 2025-2026 Appendix A Final
findings.headline: Five external audit statutory recommendations from 2024-25 remain in implementation
findings.detail: External auditors issued five statutory recommendations in March 2025 covering the council's financial position, reserves, Medium-Term Financial Strategy, and the financial considerations of bringing Homes for Lambeth in-house. Multiple actions remain ongoing as at the AGS date.
findings.matters: Statutory recommendations that remain in implementation phase indicate significant issues external audit deemed serious enough to require formal intervention
findings.figures: Five statutory recommendations issued March 2025; progress ongoing through 2025-26
findings.quote: The five statutory recommendations were considered and responded to by the Council on 5 March 2025. The recommendations relate to the Council's financial position and cover the financial year 2024-25, the budget for 2025-26 and the Medium-Term Financial Strategy period, the Council's reserves position and the Council's progress on the financial considerations of the decision to bring Homes for Lambeth in house.

findings.paper_title: Annual Governance Statement 2025-2026 Appendix A Final
findings.headline: Council reserves were substantially depleted and are being restored through asset sales to repay Exceptional Financial Support
findings.detail: Reserves had reduced substantially in recent years as the council responded to financial challenges. Exceptional Financial Support was used to restore reserves to recommended levels. The council has agreed to fund the cost of EFS through asset disposals in line with its Strategic Asset Management Framework.
findings.matters: The council's financial resilience depends on successfully executing asset disposals as planned to repay EFS; any shortfall in sale proceeds or delay in execution would create additional financial pressure
findings.figures: Reserves reduced substantially; EFS used to restore to recommended level
findings.quote: The level of reserves had reduced substantially in recent years as the Council has responded to significant financial challenges arising from service demand pressures and structural underfunding. The application of EFS to restore reserves to the recommended level enabled the Council's financial resilience to be established at an earlier opportunity than would have otherwise been the case. This was agreed on the basis that the cost of the EFS will be funded by asset disposals in line with the Council's agreed Strategic Asset Management Framework.

findings.paper_title: Annual Governance Statement 2025-2026 Appendix A Final
findings.headline: The council must deliver £46m of savings in 2026-27 to maintain financial stability
findings.detail: The 2026-27 budget approved in March 2026 includes agreed savings of £46m. The Chief Finance Officer identifies delivery of these savings as critical to the council's financial stability and resilience going forward, but execution capability in a challenging operating environment remains unproven.
findings.matters: This is a very substantial savings requirement that the council has identified as critical but has not yet demonstrated delivery capability for, particularly given control weaknesses and demand pressures in the services where savings must come from
findings.figures: £46m of agreed savings required for 2026-27
findings.quote: The delivery of the Budget 2026-27, within its resource envelope, including the agreed savings of £46m, which was approved by Council in March 2026, is critical to the financial stability and resilience of the Council.

findings.paper_title: Annual Governance Statement 2025-2026 Appendix A Final
findings.headline: Temporary accommodation and social care demand is creating significant General Fund overspends
findings.detail: The council faces sustained demand increases in temporary accommodation and social care that are stretching the availability of properties and placements. These demand-led pressures are the primary driver of the council's General Fund financial difficulties and the need for Exceptional Financial Support.
findings.matters: These are structural service pressures that are not being absorbed by available resources and are the root cause of the council's financial sustainability challenge, with no obvious containment mechanisms
findings.figures: Increasing demand in temporary accommodation and social care driving significant General Fund overspends
findings.quote: These pressures are most evident in high-demand services such as temporary accommodation and social care, where increasing demand is stretching the availability of resources, including properties and placements, and contributing to significant financial pressures within the Council's General Fund.

findings.paper_title: Annual Governance Statement 2025-2026 Appendix A Final
findings.headline: Lambeth is in receipt of Exceptional Financial Support for the General Fund and is implementing a financial sustainability plan
findings.detail: The council has applied for Exceptional Financial Support (EFS) for the General Fund for three consecutive financial years (2024-25, 2025-26, 2026-27) due to severe pressures from demand-led services. It is working on a plan to restore financial sustainability through a significant savings and transformation programme and asset disposals.
findings.matters: EFS indicates central government has assessed the council's financial position as requiring emergency support, signalling severe financial distress beyond normal budget pressures and raising fundamental questions about financial sustainability
findings.figures: Exceptional Financial Support approved for 2024-25, 2025-26, and 2026-27
findings.quote: The council is in receipt of Exceptional Financial Support in relation to the General Fund and is working on the plan to restore financial sustainability through a significant savings and transformation programme and asset disposals.

findings.paper_title: Internal Audit Annual Report and Conclusion 2025-26
findings.headline: Tenancy Management Organisations show consistently weaker control environments, representing heightened governance and oversight risk
findings.detail: TMO audits indicate consistently weaker control environments within these organisations. While these fall outside direct council control, they represent an area of heightened governance and oversight risk. Of three TMOs audited, two received Limited assurance and one received None.
findings.matters: TMOs manage council-owned housing and represent contingent governance risk. Weak controls in these entities can lead to cost overruns, service failures affecting tenants, and reputational damage to the council. Lenders may hold TMO debt or view them as a liability claim.
findings.figures: Three TMOs audited: Cottington Close (Limited); Loughborough Estate Management Board (None); Wellington Mills (Limited)
findings.quote: TMO audits indicate consistently weaker control environments within these organisations. While these fall outside direct council control, they represent an area of heightened governance and oversight risk, reflected in the overall assessment of uneven assurance across the control environment

findings.paper_title: Internal Audit Annual Report and Conclusion 2025-26
findings.headline: Cyber security controls assessed as limited; core arrangements in place but critical elements of control maturity require strengthening
findings.detail: Cyber security received a Limited assurance rating on both design and operation. Core cyber security arrangements and governance are in place, but important elements of control maturity and assurance require strengthening. The audit notes improvement is needed to embed a more consistent, proactive and regularly reviewed approach to cyber resilience across the Council.
findings.matters: Weak cyber controls create operational and financial risk: service disruption threatens revenue collection, data loss exposure creates reputational and legal liability, and ransomware incidents have bankrupted councils. This is a control environment gap in a council already under financial stress.
findings.figures: Limited assurance on both design and operation of cyber security
findings.quote: Cyber Security Assurance Limited Limited Core cyber security arrangements and governance are in place, but important elements of control maturity and assurance require strengthening. Improvement is needed to embed a more consistent, proactive and regularly reviewed approach to cyber resilience across the Council.

findings.paper_title: Internal Audit Annual Report and Conclusion 2025-26
findings.headline: 16 medium-priority audit actions overdue by up to 461 days, with oversight and governance monitoring ongoing
findings.detail: Of all open high and medium priority actions, 16 medium-priority actions are overdue. Days overdue range from 6 to 461 days. Senior Management and the Audit Committee have maintained oversight, with directors attending assurance meetings to explain delays. Implementation rates improved to 91% for high-priority and 69% for medium-priority actions, up from 54% in 24/25.
findings.matters: Overdue audit remediation over a year old signals either weak governance response or systemic issues too entrenched to fix quickly. The fact that some actions are 461 days overdue indicates sustained control gaps.
findings.figures: 0 high-priority overdue; 16 medium-priority overdue; days overdue range from 6 to 461 days; 91% high-priority implementation rate; 69% medium-priority implementation rate
findings.quote: Of all the open High and Medium priority actions the following are overdue: Children Families & Education 0 (high) / 8 (medium); Growth & Environment 0 (high) / 8 (medium); Housing 0 (high) / 1 (medium); Resources 0 (high) / 7 (medium). Days overdue range from 6 to 461 days.

findings.paper_title: Internal Audit Annual Report and Conclusion 2025-26
findings.headline: Control weaknesses concentrated in demand-led services including homelessness, children's placements and asylum-seeking children
findings.detail: A significant proportion of limited assurance outcomes was identified in high-risk service areas subject to sustained demand pressures and operational complexity. Specific limited assurance findings include homelessness/temporary accommodation, homelessness and private rented sector offers, unaccompanied asylum-seeking children, and children's placements financial processes.
findings.matters: Weak controls in high-cost, unpredictable demand-led services—where spend can spike rapidly—directly threaten financial forecasting and budget control. These are areas where overspends propagate quickly.
findings.figures: Limited assurance ratings on: Homelessness/Temporary Accommodation; Homelessness & Private Rented Sector; Unaccompanied Asylum-Seeking Children; Children's Placements Financial Processes
findings.quote: A significant proportion of limited assurance outcomes has been identified in a number of high-risk service areas, particularly those subject to: sustained demand pressures, operational complexity, and reliance on consistent application of processes and controls.

findings.paper_title: Internal Audit Annual Report and Conclusion 2025-26
findings.headline: Council requires exceptional financial support to maintain financial sustainability
findings.detail: The approved Medium Term Financial Strategy for 2026/27 confirms Lambeth needs exceptional financial support. This reflects underlying pressures including demand-led services and the level of savings and transformation required over the medium term. The audit notes this financial context represents a significant organisational risk.
findings.matters: A council needing exceptional financial support to stay solvent is a primary concern for lenders and signals structural financial stress beyond normal budget pressures.
findings.figures: Medium Term Financial Strategy 2026/27; exceptional financial support confirmed as required
findings.quote: The approved Medium Term Financial Strategy (MTFS) and Budget for 2026/27 confirms that the Council has required exceptional financial support to maintain financial sustainability. This reflects the scale of underlying pressures, including demand-led services and the level of savings and transformation required over the medium term.

findings.paper_title: Medium Term Financial Strategy Update Report 2027-2031
findings.headline: Adult Social Care provider market facing cost and sustainability pressures
findings.detail: The council identifies sustainability of the ASC provider market as a key risk. Providers face rising costs from workforce challenges, inflation and regulatory requirements. The council's controlled approach to fee uplifts, while financially disciplined, creates uncertainty and operational risk around provider capacity and supply.
findings.matters: If the provider market destabilizes, the council's ability to commission care at sustainable cost is compromised. Market risk is structural and not directly controllable by the council.
findings.figures: Demand reached historical peak in 2024-25; complexity of support requirements increasing
findings.quote: The sustainability of the provider market remains a key risk. Providers continue to face rising costs linked to workforce challenges, inflation and regulatory requirements.

findings.paper_title: Medium Term Financial Strategy Update Report 2027-2031
findings.headline: Growth & Environment budget dependent on £4.8m of external funding in fragile economic conditions
findings.detail: The Growth and Environment directorate's budgeted external contributions—from commercial property, fee income, grants, S106 and CIL—now exceed its total expenditure budgets by £4.8m. The council explicitly notes this continuation is linked to broader economic conditions which the directorate cannot control.
findings.matters: A material portion of G&E's budget (£4.8m) is not general fund baseline funding but rather relies on external sources tied to economic conditions. Economic downturn would immediately create service pressure.
findings.figures: £4.8m of external funding contributions critical to balance
findings.quote: The directorate relies heavily on funding sources outside its general fund budget allocation. Budgeted contributions from the commercial property portfolio, fee income, charges, grants, S106 and CIL now exceed total expenditure budgets by £4.8m including contribution to Employment and Skills, making the continuation of these funding sources crucial for maintaining current activities. To some extent the continuation of these sources of funds is linked to broader economic conditions which the directorate cannot influence.

findings.paper_title: Medium Term Financial Strategy Update Report 2027-2031
findings.headline: Children's Social Care already forecasting £0.7m in-year overspend amid volatile cost base
findings.detail: Client placement costs are forecasting a £0.2m overspend and staff costs a £0.5m overspend in 2026-27, despite significant budget growth (£27.223m since 2021-22). Individual placements can cost over £1m per year. The service is experiencing recruitment and retention challenges across the sector.
findings.matters: CSC is already overspending despite major investment, and the budget is highly volatile due to the cost of complex placements. Rising workforce costs and recruitment pressures are unlikely to ease.
findings.figures: £0.2m client cost overspend forecast; £0.5m staff overspend forecast; £27.223m budget growth since 2021-22; single placements >£1m/year
findings.quote: early indications are that client costs are forecasting an overspend of £0.2m, with children's numbers remaining broadly stable, and with a forecast overspend for staff of £0.5m

findings.paper_title: Medium Term Financial Strategy Update Report 2027-2031
findings.headline: HRA received £40m Exceptional Financial Support with disrepair backlog threatening long-term sustainability
findings.detail: The Housing Revenue Account received £40m EFS in 2025-26 to balance the budget due to rising disrepair costs including contractor works, damp treatments, legal and compensation costs. The council notes that long-term HRA sustainability depends on reducing the backlog of disrepair claims, a task that requires sustained capital investment.
findings.matters: The HRA is a separate borrowing entity. A £40m support package signals acute financial strain. The disrepair backlog is a major liability with no clear timeline for resolution and implies ongoing capital pressure.
findings.figures: £40m EFS for HRA in 2025-26; provision made for future disrepair settlement costs
findings.quote: For this reason, for 2025-26 the Government agreed Exceptional Financial Support for the HRA to the value of £40m to ensure the budget would be balanced and to help deal with the backlog of Disrepair cases. The longer-term financial sustainability of the HRA depends on reducing the backlog of disrepair claims

findings.paper_title: Medium Term Financial Strategy Update Report 2027-2031
findings.headline: Dedicated Schools Grant High Needs Block in £5.5m cumulative deficit with total DSG reserve collapsed
findings.detail: DSG overall surplus fell from £10.7m to £2.2m year-on-year—an £8.5m deterioration. The High Needs Block alone carries a £5.5m cumulative deficit driven by increased costs in resource bases, special schools, and independent/non-maintained school placements.
findings.matters: DSG deficits can migrate to general fund liabilities. The High Needs Block deficit is structural and related to rising SEND demand. With overall DSG surplus now only £2.2m, capacity to absorb further pressures is minimal.
findings.figures: £2.2m total DSG surplus (down £8.5m from £10.7m); £5.5m High Needs Block cumulative deficit
findings.quote: reported a cumulative surplus on the DSG at the end of 2025-26 of £2.2m, an £8.5m decrease on the 2024-25 position of £10.7m surplus. The High Needs Block in year deficit, which ended the year with a cumulative £5.5m deficit

findings.paper_title: Medium Term Financial Strategy Update Report 2027-2031
findings.headline: Temporary Accommodation transformation savings slipping from 2026-27 to 2027-28
findings.detail: The service committed to £4.8m of savings through transformation in 2026-27, but implementation delays mean these full-year benefits will likely not be realised until 2027-28, delaying the period of financial relief by one year.
findings.matters: Slippage in savings delivery extends the period of high spend and defers relief from one of the largest budget pressures (TA peaked at 4,780 placements in 2024-25).
findings.figures: £4.8m savings, one-year delay
findings.quote: delays in implementation have created a risk that they will not be fully realised in 2026-27

findings.paper_title: Medium Term Financial Strategy Update Report 2027-2031
findings.headline: £116m of Exceptional Financial Support applied in three years with repayment via future asset sales
findings.detail: The council has applied £96m of EFS in 2024-25 and 2025-26, plus a further £20m for 2026-27. While £80.1m was one-off (replenishing reserves and provisions), the capital cost of EFS must be repaid. The council expects this will ultimately require asset disposals, with an annual revenue cost peaking at £8.4m.
findings.matters: EFS is a temporary accounting mechanism: spending is capitalized rather than expensed, but repayment is deferred and expected to come from asset sales. This reduces future borrowing capacity and commits future receipts to debt service.
findings.figures: £96m + £20m = £116m total EFS; £80.1m one-off items; £8.4m peak annual revenue cost
findings.quote: Lambeth has applied a total of £96m of EFS to the General Fund over 2024-25 and 2025-26 with a further £20m to close the balance the budget in 2026-27. It is generally expected that asset disposals will ultimately be needed to fully pay back EFS

findings.paper_title: Medium Term Financial Strategy Update Report 2027-2031
findings.headline: Fair Funding Review cliff-edge removes £37.582m of transitional protection in 2029-30
findings.detail: Transitional funding protections introduced in Fair Funding Review 2.0 phase out entirely at the end of 2029-30, creating a single-year funding shock of £37.582m compared to 2028-29. This amplifies the underlying structural deficit in the final year of the MTFS.
findings.matters: This defined, material funding cliff requires advance planning and limits the council's flexibility in later years. The shock hits when transitional protections end and could force immediate and severe service reductions.
findings.quote: In particular, the withdrawal of transitional protection means a fall of £37.582 in government funding in 2029-30 compared to 2028-29

findings.paper_title: Medium Term Financial Strategy Update Report 2027-2031
findings.headline: Unresolved cumulative budget deficit of £93.217m across 2027-30 with no identified solution
findings.detail: The council has a budget gap of £19.096m for 2027-28 alone, and a cumulative shortfall of £93.217m over the three-year MTFS period. The report notes significant challenges remain and further savings beyond the already-planned £53.193m will be necessary to set a balanced budget.
findings.matters: A three-year structural deficit of this scale suggests either further major service cuts, tax rises beyond current plans, or additional borrowing—all of which affect repayment capacity and financial resilience
findings.quote: significant challenges remain, with a cumulative funding gap of £93.217m across the remaining of the MTFS period

findings.paper_title: Appendix A: Month 2 Financial Performance Report 2026-27

findings.detail: Multiple directorates report shortfalls in capitalised salaries due to the pause in capital programme. findings.figures: Growth & Environment £0.604m Highways shortfall, £0.993m capital delivery team shortfall; across directorates £1.225m+ in related pressures

The service is attempting mitigation through closer collaboration with Adult Social Care and Housing, but this suggests a structural funding problem that continues unresolved.
findings.matters: An unfunded, growing demand-led cost that the council absorbs entirely from its own budget represents a permanent structural drain on finances with no control mechanism
findings.figures: £0.874m NRPF overspend Month 2; £0.7m overspend in 2025-26
findings.quote: This is a demand-led budget, for which the Council is not funded. The forecast overspend is a small increase from the 2025/26 outturn overspend of £0.7m.

findings.paper_title: Appendix A: Month 2 Financial Performance Report 2026-27
findings.headline: Reserves remain constrained: General Fund balance at minimum recommended level, earmarked reserves offer little financial resilience

findings.quote: Although General Fund Balance is now around the level recommended by the S151 officer (10% of net revenue expenditure), earmarked revenue reserve levels remain low and offer little financial resilience in the context of the challenges ahead.

findings.paper_title: Appendix A: Month 2 Financial Performance Report 2026-27

findings.figures: £0.891m for finance improvement programme external support via flexible capital receipts
findings.quote: For example, the report recommends the flexible use of capital receipts of £0.891m for support for the delivery of the finance improvement programme through a procurement compliant framework. findings.paper_title: Appendix A: Month 2 Financial Performance Report 2026-27

findings.quote: There is also a significant shortfall in Parks events income (£1.227m) MTFS as two major summer events are no longer proceeding due to planning issues

findings.paper_title: Appendix A: Month 2 Financial Performance Report 2026-27
findings.headline: Housing Services overspending by £4.566m as temporary accommodation savings fail to deliver
findings.detail: The baseline budget before savings was £48.6m; the forecast is in line with this baseline. The £4.5m overspend is due to non-achievement of 2026-27 savings which were expected to come from: long leases (£1m not achieved), PRS incentives (£1m not achieved despite £3m spent on incentives), and additional staff costs (£1.866m) to deliver these reductions.
findings.matters: Despite significant investment in additional staff and incentive payments, the council cannot reduce temporary accommodation costs, suggesting the underlying demand problem is not being solved and costs may continue to accumulate
findings.figures: £4.566m overspend; £1m long-lease savings not achieved; £1m PRS savings not achieved; £1.866m additional staff costs
findings.quote: The £4.5m forecast overspend is due to non-achievement of savings offered up for 2026/27. These savings are being progressed but have not been implemented and therefore are not included in the forecast. Due to the delay in their implementation the 2026/27 saving is unlikely to be achieved however it is expected that the full year savings impact on 2027/28 will be achieved.

findings.paper_title: Appendix A: Month 2 Financial Performance Report 2026-27
findings.headline: Parking income target of £6.712m is at severe risk with only £500k forecast and £6.212m gap
findings.detail: Parking income is marked Red (highest risk). Currently overspending by £6.8m due to paused schemes, increased compliance, and reduction in PaybyPhone transactions. The restructure delivering £650k savings was also paused. Without restarting paused schemes and agreeing a new programme, there is no clear mitigation.
findings.matters: A £6.2m income shortfall signals either behavioural change in how residents pay for parking, or that the council's ability to generate income from its assets is impaired
findings.figures: £6.712m target; £500k forecast; £6.212m gap; currently overspending £6.8m
findings.quote: Currently overspending by £6.8m due to paused schemes, increased compliance and a reduction in PaybyPhone transactions. Without restarting the paused schemes, and agreeing a new programme, there is no clear mitigation to address this overspend.

findings.paper_title: Appendix A: Month 2 Financial Performance Report 2026-27
findings.headline: £18.157m gap in budgeted savings delivery, with 21 schemes marked as at-risk or failed
findings.detail: Of 78 savings schemes, only 11 are fully delivered (blue status), 29 are on track (green), 10 are amber-flagged, and 21 are red-flagged as at-risk or unachievable. The worst position is Growth & Environment with £11.71m of the total £18.157m gap, driven by failed income targets.
findings.matters: Nearly £18m of planned savings are not materialising, which means the council may need to find alternative funding or reduce spending further, and raises questions about forecasting and delivery capability
findings.figures: £18.157m total savings gap; £11.71m in Growth & Environment; 21 red/amber schemes
findings.quote: The Month 2 savings gap sits at £18.157m. This is considered a worst-case scenario if no planned mitigations are successful.

findings.paper_title: Appendix A: Month 2 Financial Performance Report 2026-27
findings.headline: General Fund forecasting £10.979m overspend in Month 2, despite Exceptional Financial Support
findings.detail: The council is reporting an overspend of £10.979m at end of May 2026. This follows approval of £116m Exceptional Financial Support in February 2026, yet the council is still forecasting a significant overspend in the current year. The S151 officer states confidence in achieving balance but measures are taking time to feed through.
findings.matters: A major overspend two months into the year, despite emergency government funding, signals structural budget pressures and questions whether planned management actions will materialise
findings.figures: £10.979m General Fund overspend (Month 2); £116m EFS approved February 2026
findings.quote: The General Fund forecast overspend is £10.979m. As we did for 2025/26, we are reporting at this early stage in the year to highlight pressures and identify actions that must be taken to mitigate against these pressures at a stage when there is maximum time to impact the position.

findings.paper_title: March 26 (Q4) Financial Performance Report 2025-26
findings.headline: Reserves described as offering 'little financial resilience' in context of ongoing challenges
findings.detail: The council's reserves position improved to £114.6m by year-end (up from £93.1m opening balance through EFS top-ups), but the S151 officer explicitly states: 'Reserve levels remain low and offer little financial resilience in the context of the challenges ahead. It is therefore imperative that directorates continue to work to bring down spend and close the budget gap.' Without EFS, the overspend would have required at least £15m of reserves to be used.
findings.matters: Low reserves limit the council's ability to absorb further adverse movements. Any additional pressure would likely trigger further government support requests.
findings.figures: Closing reserves £114.613m; opening £93.069m; would have required £15m+ of reserves without EFS
findings.quote: Reserve levels remain low and offer little financial resilience in the context of the challenges ahead. It is therefore imperative that directorates continue to work to bring down spend and close the budget gap.

findings.paper_title: March 26 (Q4) Financial Performance Report 2025-26
findings.headline: Council to face independent CIPFA review and quarterly MHCLG meetings; enhanced government scrutiny regime
findings.detail: As an EFS council, Lambeth is now subject to enhanced scrutiny from MHCLG. The paper states: 'As part of this we are expecting to be notified of an independent third-party review, such as by CIPFA, in the near future. Furthermore we expect quarterly meetings with MHCLG to report on our progress in returning to a financially sustainable position.' MHCLG will focus on asset disposal progress and savings programme delivery.
findings.matters: External review and quarterly reporting regime indicates regulator concern about sustainability. CIPFA reviews often identify further issues and lead to operational intervention.
findings.figures: EFS council status; expected CIPFA review; quarterly MHCLG meetings
findings.quote: It is emphasised that as an EFS council, we will be under increased scrutiny from MHCLG. As part of this we are expecting to be notified of an independent third-party review, such as by CIPFA, in the near future. Furthermore we expect quarterly meetings with MHCLG to report on our progress in returning to a financially sustainable position.

findings.paper_title: March 26 (Q4) Financial Performance Report 2025-26
findings.headline: Capital programme underspent by 59.6% (£131.4m); £32m of schemes paused or ceased; governance acknowledged as weak
findings.detail: The capital programme underspent by £131.4m (59.6% of budget) in 2025-26. Of this, £32m was due to schemes being paused or ceased as a result of the capital review, but the majority (£100m) was due to slippage. The council explicitly acknowledges the issue: 'We are updating our capital programme processes and strengthening our governance arrangements which will reduce project delivery slippage going forward.' This suggests significant project management weakness.
findings.matters: Large underspend indicates either over-optimistic planning or delivery failure. The council's own acknowledgment of governance weakness is a red flag for capital-intensive investments or borrowing commitments.
findings.figures: £131.4m underspend (59.6%); £32m schemes paused/ceased; £100m slippage; General Fund £74m, HRA £58m
findings.quote: The capital programme has underspent by £budget in 2025-26. This is partly due to the General Fund capital review that led to circa £32m of schemes being paused or ceased, however the majority (circa £100m) is due to capital programme slippage (reprofiling of spend to future years to match delivery plans)... We are updating our capital programme processes and strengthening our governance arrangements which will reduce project delivery slippage going forward.

findings.paper_title: March 26 (Q4) Financial Performance Report 2025-26
findings.headline: DSG High Needs Block overspent by £8.9m and will move into cumulative deficit by end of 2026-27, reliant on statutory override
findings.detail: The Dedicated Schools Grant closed with an overspend of £8.475m in 2025-26, primarily driven by the High Needs Block (£8.9m overspend). This reflects ongoing demand-led pressures from Education, Health and Care Plans (EHCPs) and independent/non-maintained special school placements. The paper explicitly states the DSG 'will be in overall deficit by the end of 2026-27 and will therefore remain reliant on the DSG statutory override arrangements.' A SEND Reform Plan is being developed but linked to delivery of reforms which may or may not succeed.
findings.matters: SEND deficits represent a demand-led pressure outside council control, masked by statutory accounting override. The deficit will persist into future years and is a structural imbalance.
findings.figures: £8.475m DSG overspend in 2025-26; £8.9m High Needs Block overspend; DSG will be in deficit by end 2026-27
findings.quote: The DSG will be in overall deficit by the end of 2026-27 and will therefore remain reliant on the DSG statutory override arrangements, which allow deficits to be held separately from the Council's General Fund. The Council is developing a SEND Reform Plan as required by the Department of Education, aimed at improving outcomes for children and young people with SEND and supporting the long-term sustainability of High Needs spending.

findings.paper_title: March 26 (Q4) Financial Performance Report 2025-26
findings.headline: Housing temporary accommodation overspend of £14.5m; highest single directorate pressure despite management action
findings.detail: Housing Services reports an overspend of £14.528m, with temporary accommodation (TA) accounting for the majority of the budget. Nightly-paid TA alone overspent by £8.5m. Although this is an improvement of £3.5m from Q3 due to management actions (prevention, incentive schemes, move-on support), it remains the council's largest budget pressure. The council has deployed additional staff (£5.1m overspend) specifically to manage TA reduction.
findings.matters: Demonstrates persistent homelessness/TA demand that management action is only partially containing. This is a demand-led pressure that may not be controllable by the council.
findings.figures: £14.528m total overspend; £8.546m nightly-paid TA overspend; £5.109m additional staff costs for TA reduction; £1.282m incentive scheme costs
findings.quote: TA accounts for the majority of the Housing Services budget and spend. During the year there has been a continued reduction in the number of households in TA. This reflects management action to 1) prevent households entering TA 2) support move on from TA into more sustainable Private Rented Sector (PRS) accommodation through incentive schemes 3) facilitate transfers into more cost-effective accommodation options and 4) the introduction of charging for emergency accommodation.

findings.paper_title: March 26 (Q4) Financial Performance Report 2025-26
findings.headline: Major savings programme delivering only 46% of planned reductions; £14.9m Target Operating Model saving deferred to 2026-27
findings.detail: The council planned to deliver £46.3m of savings in 2025-26 but achieved only £21.3m, leaving a gap of £24.9m. The largest deferred item is the £14.87m Target Operating Model (TOM) saving, which has been 'reprofiled into 2026-27 to link to specific programmes of work.' Growth & Environment faces a £7.5m savings gap out of £16.9m planned, and Resources has a £1.7m gap out of £2.5m planned.
findings.matters: Non-delivery of structural cost reductions undermines the credibility of the council's financial recovery plan. Reprofiling to 2026-27 suggests the transformation is lagging schedule.
findings.figures: £24.956m gap out of £46.296m target (54% undelivered); TOM saving of £14.87m deferred; Growth & Environment gap £7.481m; Resources gap £1.743m
findings.quote: There is a £24.956m gap between savings proposed and likely delivered, £14.87m of which is the Target Operating Model saving. The required saving from the TOM has been reprofiled into 2026-27 to link to specific programmes of work which will be monitored individually from 2026-27 onwards.

findings.paper_title: March 26 (Q4) Financial Performance Report 2025-26
findings.headline: Council approved for £116m government bailout due to inability to balance budget from own resources
findings.detail: In February 2026, MHCLG approved £116m of Exceptional Financial Support (EFS) across three years (2024-25 to 2026-27) in declining amounts. This allows capitalisation of revenue spending to be financed through borrowing or asset sales. The S151 officer states they are confident the council can return to balance, but 'measures put in place and reviews underway will take time to feed through and some support will be required in the meantime.'
findings.matters: A council requiring government bailout is a material credit risk indicator. This signals structural deficit not addressable within the council's own budget.
findings.figures: £116m EFS across three years; £46m GF EFS used in 2025-26 and 2024-25 combined; total £96m GF EFS
findings.quote: In February 2026, the Council's application for £116m of Exceptional Financial Support (EFS) was approved in principle by MHCLG. The £116m was for support across the three years 2024-25 through to 2026-27 in declining amounts.

findings.paper_title: Appendix A - updated key risk summary Q4 25-26
findings.headline: Multiple regulatory compliance areas have only limited assurance from internal audit, particularly housing, homelessness, and children's services
findings.detail: Internal audit has issued Limited Assurance ratings on five high-risk compliance areas: No recourse to Public Funds, Temporary Accommodation Review and Move-on, Homelessness/Temporary Accommodation, Unaccompanied Asylum-Seeking Children, and Health and Safety in Children's Settings. The second line assessment states the council 'faces significant challenges in complying with an increasing and more rigorous regulatory regime, particularly regarding housing standards and financial management.'
findings.matters: Limited assurance in high-risk service areas (housing, homelessness, children's) indicates inadequate control environment. This creates regulatory, legal, and reputational risk, confirmed by the council's existing disrepair litigation and Awaab's Law compliance obligations.
findings.figures: 5 areas with Limited Assurance from internal audit
findings.quote: The council faces significant challenges in complying with an increasing and more rigorous regulatory regime, particularly regarding housing standards and financial management.

findings.paper_title: Appendix A - updated key risk summary Q4 25-26
findings.headline: Housing stock maintenance is being deferred due to financial pressures, creating health and safety risks to tenants and stock deterioration
findings.detail: The risk assessment identifies potential deferral of essential maintenance due to financial constraints, creating health and safety hazards. This reflects the tension between HRA underfunding (rent caps limit income growth) and maintenance obligations. To address regulatory risk, an Awaab's Law readiness group with 8 workstreams has been established, and a Disrepair Case Reduction Action Plan runs through 2027, indicating ongoing litigation exposure.
findings.matters: Deferred housing maintenance creates tenant safety liability, regulatory exposure under Awaab's Law (emergency ventilation/damp requirements), litigation risk from disrepair claims, and long-term unplanned capital needs. Disrepair case reductions are necessary but indicate current failures.
findings.figures: Awaab's Law readiness group with 8 workstreams; Disrepair Case Reduction Action Plan 2025-27
findings.quote: Essential maintenance not being undertaken providing health & safety risks to tenants; deterioration of Housing Stock.

findings.paper_title: Appendix A - updated key risk summary Q4 25-26
findings.headline: Temporary accommodation demand stabilised in 2025-26, but Finance Director warns stability is at risk of not being sustained
findings.detail: During 2025-26, demand in temporary accommodation and adults/children's services seemed to stabilise following earlier high-demand periods. However, the Finance Director specifically notes 'risk that this will not be sustained in the current year' and flags that 'continued close monitoring & management actions will be required'. Cost of living impacts are cited as an ongoing driver of temporary accommodation and social housing demand.
findings.matters: Temporary accommodation is a high-cost, controllable cost driver. If demand re-emerges after apparent stabilisation, it would create unbudgeted cost pressures and challenge revenue forecasts. The Finance Director's caution suggests internal uncertainty about sustainability.
findings.figures: High demand areas identified but specific outturn not quantified
findings.quote: During 2025/26 pressures in the high demand areas of temporary accommodation, adults & children's services have seemed to stabilise indicating that actions taken are having an impact. There remains a risk that this will not be sustained in the current year and continued close monitoring & management actions will be required.

findings.paper_title: Appendix A - updated key risk summary Q4 25-26
findings.headline: Capital programme review and spend control panel have reduced planned borrowing by £135 million, indicating previous over-commitment
findings.detail: Management has implemented a fundamental review of the capital programme and updated capital and treasury strategies to reduce external debt. The spend control panel has helped reduce borrowing significantly below previous forecasts, creating a positive MTFS impact. However, the magnitude of the reduction (£135 million) indicates that earlier capital planning was overcommitted and discipline was weak.
findings.matters: While the reduction is positive for near-term debt targets, it confirms capital planning controls were previously deficient. Lenders need confidence that the revised capital strategy will be adhered to and not require further material reductions.
findings.figures: £135 million borrowing reduction from capital project reviews
findings.quote: management has implemented recruitment freezes, reviews of capital projects (reducing borrowing by £135 million), and reduced senior management costs to mitigate pressures

findings.paper_title: Appendix A - updated key risk summary Q4 25-26
findings.headline: The council faces a critically adverse financial position with underfunding, inadequate reserves, and sustained cost pressures
findings.detail: Lambeth's critical financial position remains rated High (32), unchanged from inherent rating, with only a Medium (12) target by end-of-period. Causes include structural underfunding from the Local Government Finance Settlement not keeping pace with inflation, sustained cost pressures in temporary accommodation and social care, HRA underfunding due to rent caps on income, and Building Safety Act and Decent Homes Standard mandates increasing expenditure without matching funding. Risk of Section 114 (statutory insolvency) is explicitly cited as a potential outcome.
findings.matters: Critically adverse financial position with inadequate reserves creates immediate refinancing risk. The potential for Section 114 is a material credit event affecting the council's ability to borrow and deliver services.
findings.figures: Risk rating High (32) current / High (32) inherent / Medium (12) target
findings.quote: The council faces a critically adverse financial position, with underfunding, inadequate reserves, and sustained cost pressures across key Lambeth 2030 Ambitions and service areas.

findings.paper_title: 0.Treasury Management Performance Report at 31-03-26 (DRAFT)
findings.headline: Internal borrowing increased by £67.4m to £180.2m, significantly depleting cash reserves
findings.detail: The council's estimated internal borrowing (using cash balances instead of external borrowing) increased from £112.75m in 2024/25 to £180.15m in 2025/26 — a 60% increase. This strategy erodes the council's liquidity buffer; when cash runs out, the council must return to external borrowing at prevailing (currently elevated) interest rates.
findings.matters: While internal borrowing avoids taking on new external debt, it depletes the cash position that provides flexibility for unexpected costs or falling revenues; the trend suggests the council is approaching the limits of this approach.

findings.quote: Estimated Internal Borrowing 112,750 ... Forecast 2025/26 ... 180,150 Change 67,400

findings.paper_title: 0.Treasury Management Performance Report at 31-03-26 (DRAFT)
findings.headline: £30m property investment maturing 31 July 2026 with no clear reinvestment plan disclosed
findings.detail: Lambeth invested £30m in Resonance Limited's Real Lettings Property Fund 2. The fund had a 9-year life and is now in extension period, due to mature 31 July 2026. The council received £0.68m income in the year ending 31 March 2026. The report states only that 'consideration is currently underway in relation to future investment in the Fund' with no clarity on how the £30m proceeds will be deployed.
findings.matters: A £30m maturity is a material capital event; if the council has no clear redeploy plan, proceeds may sit idle or force external borrowing, affecting liquidity and borrowing costs.
findings.figures: £30m invested; £0.68m income in year ending 31 March 2026; maturity date 31 July 2026

findings.paper_title: 0.Treasury Management Performance Report at 31-03-26 (DRAFT)
findings.headline: Long-term borrowing rates have risen and rate-cut forecasts pushed back to Q3 2027

findings.headline: Interest costs overran budget by £5.7m (13.7%)

findings.quote: The interest payable on external borrowing for the year ending 31 March 2026 was £47.2m, against a budget of £41.5m.

findings.paper_title: 0.Treasury Management Performance Report at 31-03-26 (DRAFT)
findings.headline: Council received £116m Exceptional Financial Support from MHCLG to work towards sustainable finances
findings.detail: Application for £116m EFS was approved by MHCLG. The council plans to fund it from capital receipts to minimise revenue impact, but may need to borrow in the shorter term, adding to future debt burden. This signals the council had significant financial difficulty requiring government intervention.

findings.figures: £116m EFS approved

findings.paper_title: London Borough of Lambeth_2025.26_Forvis Mazars_Audit Status Report May 2026 (updated)
findings.headline: Auditor cannot adopt efficient proof-in-total approach; must use more resource-intensive historic testing instead.
findings.detail: Due to high-risk assessment and material difficulties in the prior two years, auditors cannot use the streamlined proof-in-total method for rebuilding assurance. They must instead undertake substantive testing of historic transactions from the disclaimed years to establish opening balances.
findings.matters: Historic testing is significantly more resource-intensive and will take longer. This delays return to an unqualified opinion and signals auditor concerns about the reliability of the council's prior year positions.
findings.figures: No figures given
findings.quote: We will be required to adopt the historic testing approach to re-building assurance

findings.paper_title: London Borough of Lambeth_2025.26_Forvis Mazars_Audit Status Report May 2026 (updated)
findings.headline: Council failed to meet standard audit turnaround timeframes and lacked accountability for delivery.
findings.detail: Despite improvements from the new Chief Accountant in January/February 2026, the council was unable to provide working papers, data, and audit responses within expected timeframes. There was no clear process to escalate non-delivery to senior management or assign ownership of audit areas.
findings.matters: Weak audit responsiveness and accountability indicate broader finance team capability issues. The need to escalate non-delivery to Chief Executive level suggests systemic management problems.
findings.figures: No specific delays quantified; agreed standard turnarounds are: data in line with PBC schedule, sample evidence within 4 working days, queries within 48 hours
findings.quote: Whilst improvements were made in January and February 2026, the Council were unable to operate in line with expected timeframes for the provision of working papers, data requests and audit query responses. This prevented the audit team planning the effective use of resources and executing the audit efficiently

findings.paper_title: London Borough of Lambeth_2025.26_Forvis Mazars_Audit Status Report May 2026 (updated)
findings.headline: Working papers lacked audit trails, contained errors, and required substantial rework.
findings.detail: The council submitted working papers with no clear link to financial statement balances, missing explanatory narratives, and internal errors. This forced auditors to spend significantly more time on queries and procedures than planned, delaying the audit.
findings.matters: The quality of working papers reflects the council's financial control environment and accounting expertise. Weak working papers indicate systemic issues in how the council records, reconciles, and explains its transactions.
findings.figures: No figures given
findings.quote: In several instances, the Council's working papers provided no clear audit trail between the workings and the financial statement balance being audited. In other instances, working papers contained errors, or included no narrative to enable the auditors to understand and interpret their contents

findings.matters: Council subsidiaries often hold significant assets or liabilities that feed into group accounts. Problems there amplify risks in the consolidated position and suggest control weaknesses across the whole organisation.
findings.figures: Specific issues not detailed
findings.quote: The issues reported by the Council's subsidiary companies (the HFL entities) for 2024/25 and the Council's worsening financial health during the disclaimed years compound this risk

findings.matters: Reserve adequacy is the primary indicator of a council's financial sustainability and borrowing headroom. Growing pressure on reserves while unable to demonstrate accurate accounting is a critical concern for lenders.

findings.quote: the Council's financial challenges increasing pressure on reserves, there is a higher risk of material misstatement in respect of opening reserve balances

They cite the Council's challenges in preparing materially accurate accounts and resource constraints as reasons for deferring rebuilding assurance to 2026/27.

We will therefore issue a disclaimed audit opinion on the 2025/26 accounts and aim to do this by the end of November

findings.paper_title: 06. Lambeth Pension Fund Actuarial Valuation Results 2026 and FSS
findings.headline: Pension fund funding level surged to 120%, moving from 96% funded and a deficit to 120% funded with a £297m surplus
findings.detail: Past service liabilities fell £416m to £1,504m while assets remained relatively stable at £1,800m. The improvement is attributed to increased expected future investment performance using a 5.5% discount rate, with an 85% likelihood of achieving this return over the next 20 years.
findings.matters: A strong surplus substantially reduces the risk of future contribution rate increases or special funding calls, improving long-term budget certainty.
findings.figures: Funding level 120% (from 96%); surplus £297m (from deficit of £79m); liabilities £1,504m (from £1,920m)
findings.quote: The funding level has increased by 24% over the valuation period, largely as a result of an increase in the Fund's expected future investment performance. It is based on a discount rate, or future investment rate of return, of 5.5% p.a., and there is a 85% likelihood of achieving this level of annual return over the next 20 years.

findings.paper_title: 06. Lambeth Pension Fund Actuarial Valuation Results 2026 and FSS
findings.headline: Secondary contribution rates shifted from positive payments to negative refunds over three years
findings.detail: The fund moved from requiring additional employer payments (£6.9-7.2m/year) to paying back contributions to employers (£2.4-6.7m/year). Due to the fund's strong surplus, employers including Lambeth will see overall contribution rate reductions of around 5% over the three-year period.
findings.matters: This reversal improves employer cash flow significantly and signals reduced long-term pension liabilities for the council's financial planning.
findings.quote: Due to the strong surplus, the Fund is able to apply a negative Secondary Rate. Given this positive funding position, most other employers in the Fund will see contribution rate reductions of around 5% over the three-year period.

findings.paper_title: 06. Lambeth Pension Fund Actuarial Valuation Results 2026 and FSS
findings.headline: Primary contribution rate increased to 22.1% of pay, up from 20.7%
findings.detail: The cost of building new pension benefits has increased by 1.4 percentage points of payroll. This represents a direct cost pressure on the council's pension contributions to employees.
findings.matters: Pension contributions are a material fixed cost on payroll; an increase directly reduces available budget or requires additional savings elsewhere.
findings.quote: The Primary Rate (the cost of building new benefits) has increased to 22.1% of pay (from 20.7%).

findings.paper_title: Appendix 04 - Agreed Savings 2026-30
findings.headline: Temporary accommodation savings of £15.997m depend critically on procurement of long-lease units and moving residents to private rented sector
findings.detail: Housing's largest savings programme (the council's second-largest directorate savings) includes ending hotel use for temporary accommodation (£1.2m, one year), procuring long-lease units (£5.7m over four years), and supporting residents into private rented sector (£6m in years 2 and 3 only). The private sector placement generates £3m per year in years 2-3 but £0 in years 1 and 4.
findings.matters: Temporary accommodation is often volatile and demand-driven. This restructuring is ambitious—success depends on unit availability at budgeted cost and landlord willingness to accept placed residents. If procurement or placement underperforms, the council faces a £3-6m annual gap in years 2-3.
findings.figures: £15,997m total Housing savings; £5.7m from long-lease procurement; £6m from private sector placement (£3m each in 2027-28 and 2028-29)
findings.quote: Temporary accommodation procurement of units on long leases 1,100 2,300 2,300 0 5,700 and Supporting people in temporary accommodation into the private rented sector 0 3,000 3,000 0 6,000

findings.paper_title: Appendix 04 - Agreed Savings 2026-30
findings.headline: Growth and Environment directorate contributes £8.384m entirely in 2026-27 with zero savings in subsequent years, raising sustainability questions
findings.detail: Growth & Environment accounts for 18% of new agreed savings (£8.384m) but all are scheduled for 2026-27 only. Later years show '-' for this directorate. Items include parking charge reviews (£1.5m), regulatory services restructure (£1.061m), parks operations restructure (£702k), and various service reductions. Most would be expected to generate recurring savings if implemented.
findings.matters: A lender assessing financial stability needs to know if the council has identified sustainable multi-year savings or is relying on front-loaded, potentially one-off items. If Growth & Environment savings plateau here while other directorates carry forward, future years may have a shortfall.
findings.quote: Growth and Environment total 8,384 - - - 8,384

findings.paper_title: Appendix 09 - Treasury Management Strategy 2026-27
findings.headline: Almost one-third of debt portfolio matures within five years, exposed to refinancing risk if rate cuts do not occur
findings.detail: The debt maturity profile shows 30.51% of borrowing due to mature within five years (12.27% under 12 months, 3.81% at 12-24 months, 14.43% at 24-60 months). Current weighted interest rate is 4.21%. Debt rescheduling is currently unviable due to large gaps between premature redemption rates and new borrowing rates.
findings.matters: If forecasted rate reductions to 3.25% by end 2026-27 do not materialise, refinancing of maturing debt at sustained or higher rates would significantly increase interest costs and worsen affordability
findings.figures: £1,137.7m external borrowing at 4.21% weighted average rate; 30.51% due within 5 years
