findings.paper_title: Appendix 09 - Treasury Management Strategy 2026-27
findings.headline: Financing costs as percentage of net revenue rising to 12.95% by 2028-29, sharply reducing budget flexibility
findings.detail: The General Fund ratio of financing costs to net revenue is forecast to rise from 10.37% in 2025-26 to 12.95% in 2028-29, increasing year-on-year. This shows an accelerating proportion of the revenue budget consumed by debt service, leaving diminishing room for other pressures.
findings.matters: At ratios above 12%, councils have minimal financial flexibility to manage unexpected costs or invest in service improvements; rising trend indicates worsening affordability
findings.quote: GF ratio of financing costs to revenue (%) 10.37%  12.47% 12.72% 12.95%

findings.paper_title: Appendix 09 - Treasury Management Strategy 2026-27
findings.headline: Homes for Lambeth £36.7m loan book undergoing external review with outcome deferred to summer 2026, following Kerslake Report impairments
findings.detail: Following the Kerslake Report, impairments have been taken on HfL loans. Outstanding loans stand at £36.7m as at 31 December 2025. External consultants and legal advisors have been appointed to review the future of the four HfL companies, with outcome expected in late spring/early summer 2026. The review indicates complexity and uncertainty about whether the loan book will be recovered.
findings.matters: Further impairments are possible; appointment of external advisors and deferred outcome signals material uncertainty about loan recovery and adds to professional fees during financial stress
findings.figures: £36.7m outstanding HfL loan balance as at 31 December 2025
findings.quote: External consultants and legal advisors have been appointed to assist the Council. The outcome of the review is expected in late spring/early summer 2026.

findings.paper_title: Appendix 09 - Treasury Management Strategy 2026-27
findings.headline: Council using £359m of reserve cash instead of external borrowing, depleting financial buffers
findings.detail: As at 31 March 2026, the council is internally borrowed by £359m (27% of underlying borrowing requirement), meaning cash backing reserves and balances has been used instead of taking external loans. The paper notes that cash balances have fallen in recent years to support this position.
findings.matters: Internal borrowing from reserves is unsustainable; once cash balances are exhausted, the council will be forced to externalize this borrowing, sharply increasing external debt and interest costs
findings.figures: £359m internal borrowing; 27% of underlying borrowing requirement
findings.quote: As at 31 March 2026 the council is forecast to be internally borrowed by £359 million, which means cash backing up reserves and balances as well as working capital has been used in lieu of external borrowing, accounting for 27% of the underlying borrowing requirement.

findings.paper_title: Appendix 09 - Treasury Management Strategy 2026-27
findings.headline: Exceptional Financial Support application of £116m submitted, indicating council cannot balance budget without government approval
findings.detail: The council has submitted an EFS application of £116m, which would allow it to borrow or use capital receipts to fund revenue costs. EFS is granted only when councils cannot achieve financial sustainability through normal means. The council aims to fund this from capital receipts but acknowledges it may need to be met from borrowing in the shorter term.
findings.matters: EFS signals structural financial difficulties; the council cannot achieve budget balance independently and is dependent on government approval of exceptional measures
findings.figures: £116m EFS application
findings.quote: An application for £116m of EFS has been submitted. If approved, this will allow the council to borrow or use capital receipts to fund revenue costs while it works towards a more sustainable financial position.

findings.paper_title: Appendix 09a - LB Lambeth - capital strategy
findings.headline: Strict spending controls introduced: 20% senior management reduction, recruitment freeze, agency staff cuts, and pause on non-essential capital.
findings.detail: In response to financial pressures, the council has 'Implemented strict spending controls and cost reductions including a 20% reduction in senior management, a freeze on non-essential recruitment, reductions in agency staff and a pause on capital expenditure funded from borrowing other than to meet contractual commitments or critical statutory duties.'
findings.matters: Organisational restructuring and spending freezes, while necessary, can degrade service delivery, management capacity, and institutional knowledge; they may indicate distress mode management rather than strategic improvement.
findings.figures: 20% reduction in senior management; freeze on non-essential recruitment
findings.quote: Implemented strict spending controls and cost reductions including a 20% reduction in senior management, a freeze on non-essential recruitment, reductions in agency staff and a pause on capital expenditure funded from borrowing other than to meet contractual commitments or critical statutory duties.

findings.paper_title: Appendix 09a - LB Lambeth - capital strategy
findings.headline: Structural underfunding: the council has 35% less per resident to spend than in 2010, with rising demand for statutory services.
findings.detail: The council notes it faces 'significant financial pressures as a result of structural underfunding from central government since 2010. We have 35% less per resident to spend than we did in 2010.' Over the same decade, demand and complexity of need in the population has increased, particularly for temporary accommodation for homeless families and adult and children's social care.
findings.matters: Structural underfunding combined with rising demand for statutory services creates a persistent imbalance; this is not cyclical and cannot be resolved without radical service change or external subsidy.
findings.figures: 35% reduction in per-resident spending since 2010; rising costs in temporary accommodation and social care
findings.quote: This strategy is set against a background of the council facing significant financial pressures as a result of structural underfunding from central government since 2010. We have 35% less per resident to spend than we did in 2010.

findings.paper_title: Appendix 09a - LB Lambeth - capital strategy
findings.headline: Council fundamentally changed capital strategy: borrowing is now explicitly 'a last resort', ending a decade of borrowing-led capital investment.
findings.detail: The council states: 'In the previous Capital Strategy, the view was that the Council would be able to afford to make up the shortfall between capital investment and funding with borrowing. This is no longer the intention given the financial position of the Council and will only be considered as a last resort.' The council has also implemented a pause on capital expenditure funded from borrowing except for contractual commitments or critical statutory duties.
findings.matters: This signals a fundamental shift in the council's financial strategy; lenders need to know that future capital investment will be severely constrained and dependent on external grants and receipts rather than borrowing.
findings.figures: 2025-26 to 2027-28: £94m of £211m (44%) capital programme funded by borrowing, now to be avoided
findings.quote: In the previous Capital Strategy, the view was that the Council would be able to afford to make up the shortfall between capital investment and funding with borrowing. This is no longer the intention given the financial position of the Council and will only be considered as a last resort.

findings.paper_title: Appendix 09a - LB Lambeth - capital strategy
findings.headline: Capital programme slippage averages 30% annually; only 70% of budget is spent per year, with the council now focusing on reducing this delivery gap.
findings.detail: Across the last decade, only 70% of the capital investment programme budget has been spent in a given year, with the balance carried forward. Delivery varies, though average annual spend is £140m. The council has created a £2m Feasibility Reserve and is implementing more realistic annual profiling to address this slippage.
findings.matters: Persistent slippage indicates weak project delivery capability or overly ambitious planning; it delays infrastructure investment and can signal organisational dysfunction.
findings.figures: 70% budget delivery rate per year; £140m average annual spend over last decade
findings.quote: The ten-year trend in capital investment and how it has been funded / financed shows that in general only 70% of the capital investment programme / capital budget has been spent in a given year, with the balance carried forward.

findings.paper_title: Appendix 09a - LB Lambeth - capital strategy
findings.headline: Debt servicing costs are rising, reflecting a decade of increased borrowing now totalling at least £1,034m in key investment areas.
findings.detail: The council explicitly identifies rising debt servicing and interest costs as a focus. Figure 2 shows historic interest payable trends. Borrowing has increased significantly across 2014-15 to 2024-25. Table 5 shows £1,034m in borrowing used for housing improvements (£495m), redress scheme (£170m), leaseholder buy-back (£132m), housing loans (£132m), and town hall consolidation (£105m).
findings.matters: Rising debt service reduces the council's financial flexibility and diverts resources from service delivery; a lender needs to understand the trajectory of interest costs and whether revenue can support them.
findings.figures: £1,034m total borrowing (HRA £495m, General Fund £539m); historic annual spend averages £140m, with ~70% delivered per year
findings.quote: A focus in our strategy will be debt servicing/interest costs, which are rising, reflecting the increasing level of borrowing over the last decade.

findings.paper_title: Appendix 09a - LB Lambeth - capital strategy
findings.headline: HRA reserves have fallen below the minimum prudent level and received £40m capitalisation directive, driven by legacy housing disrepair claims.
findings.detail: The Housing Revenue Account (ring-fenced housing service) has seen its reserves reduced to below the minimum prudent level. It received EFS of £40m in 2025-26 as a capitalisation directive due to financial pressures driven by a high volume of legacy housing disrepair claims. The council is using temporary borrowing to finance this EFS.
findings.matters: The HRA is ring-fenced, so its insolvency poses specific risk to housing tenants and the council's ability to invest in its 23,600-unit housing stock; legacy claims indicate unquantified future liabilities.
findings.figures: £40m capitalisation directive for HRA 2025-26
findings.quote: The Council has also seen its Housing Revenue Account (HRA) reserves reduced to below the minimum prudent level and has EFS in 2025-26, to manage the financial pressures which have been driven by a high volume of legacy housing disrepair claims.

findings.paper_title: Appendix 09a - LB Lambeth - capital strategy
findings.headline: General Fund received £116m Exceptional Financial Support, covering three years of revenue spending shortfall.
findings.detail: The council approached government for EFS of £116m in December 2025 to cover 2024-25 to 2026-27, including retrospectively replenishing reserves. The intention is to repay from capital receipts over the medium term. The council has made provision for capital financing costs in its budgets.
findings.matters: A lender needs to know the council cannot fund its operations from revenue and is dependent on government support to meet day-to-day expenditure; this is a material solvency indicator.
findings.figures: £116m EFS for General Fund; covers 2024-25 to 2026-27
findings.quote: Approached the Government for Exceptional Financial Support (EFS) of £116m for the GF in December 2025. This is to cover the period 2024-25 to 2026-27, and as such includes retrospectively replenishing reserves.

findings.paper_title: Appendix 12 - Section 25 Assurance Statement 26.27
findings.headline: Homes for Lambeth companies facing external audit recommendation and potential balance-sheet impact
findings.detail: External auditors issued a statutory recommendation in February 2025 that the council bring housing provision back in-house rather than continue with Homes for Lambeth group companies (HfL Group, HfL Build, HfL Homes, HfL Living). The financial consequences are still being worked through with external advisors. Options will be presented in summer 2026 and may significantly impact the MTFS and balance sheet.
findings.matters: An external audit recommendation to restructure a major operational subsidiary suggests current governance arrangements are not sustainable; the financial impact of unwinding these structures is currently unknown.
findings.figures: No specific figures disclosed yet; analysis ongoing
findings.quote: In February 2025, the Council's external auditors issued a statutory recommendation to i) take further action to implement the key recommendation of the Kerslake report: to bring the provision of housing services back 'in-house'

findings.paper_title: Appendix 12 - Section 25 Assurance Statement 26.27
findings.headline: Lambeth is 'one of the worst affected' by new government funding formula
findings.detail: The Final Local Government Settlement, published February 2026, includes a new funding formula that significantly disadvantages inner-London boroughs. Lambeth is explicitly identified as one of the worst-affected councils. Transitional protection mitigates this somewhat until 2028-29, but the underlying needs assessment reduces the council's baseline allocation.
findings.matters: A council facing structural underfunding relative to demographic need will struggle to balance budgets without service cuts or tax rises; this signals long-term financial stress.
findings.figures: Multi-year settlement to 2028-29; Lambeth identified as one of worst-affected inner London boroughs
findings.quote: based on an updated assessment of relative needs, inner-London boroughs overall see a decline in the level of funding received, with Lambeth being one of the worst affected.

findings.paper_title: Appendix 12 - Section 25 Assurance Statement 26.27
findings.headline: Housing Revenue Account reserves exhausted; 2025-26 only balanced via EFS
findings.detail: The HRA has been under severe financial pressure for years and has almost entirely exhausted its reserves. In 2025-26, the budget could only be balanced using a £40m EFS capitalisation direction from government. Future pressures from aging housing stock maintenance and disrepair cases loom. The council is developing a 30-year HRA business plan but recovery is not assured.
findings.matters: HRA insolvency signals the council cannot sustain its housing stock or meet landlord obligations without continued government support; this affects both credit risk and delivery of council services.
findings.figures: £40m EFS capitalisation direction for HRA in 2025-26; HRA reserves almost entirely exhausted
findings.quote: The HRA has been under considerable financial pressure in recent years and has almost entirely exhausted its reserves.

findings.paper_title: Appendix 12 - Section 25 Assurance Statement 26.27
findings.headline: Income collection risks require £4m provision, particularly from car parking
findings.detail: The council has identified that bad debt provisions were historically insufficient. Car parking income was identified as the main risk area. A £4m provision has been set aside to mitigate income collection risks. This suggests the council has experienced or anticipates difficulty collecting non-social-care income streams.
findings.matters: Increasing bad debt provisions indicate deteriorating collection, possibly reflecting economic distress in the borough; lenders track whether income assumptions are realistic.
findings.figures: £4m provision for non-collection of income
findings.quote: Whilst EFS looks to improve the Council's resilience by providing the capacity to increase provisions in relation to car parking income, which was the main risk area, there remains a risk in relation to other income sources. A provision of £4m has been set aside to mitigate against this risk.

findings.paper_title: Appendix 12 - Section 25 Assurance Statement 26.27
findings.headline: £46.6m savings programme for 2026-27 carries significant delivery risk
findings.detail: The 2026-27 budget depends on delivering £46.6m of savings, a substantial programme. Although plans are in place, the S151 officer acknowledges material risk around timely delivery of such a large-scale programme. A £14m contingency provision has been set aside, but this only covers exceptional circumstances—suggesting expectations that most savings should materialize.
findings.matters: Large savings programmes frequently encounter delays and partial delivery; if this £46.6m is not realized, the council will return to deficit despite EFS support.
findings.figures: £46.6m savings target; £14m contingency provision for non-delivery
findings.quote: The 2026-27 budget is built on the assumption of the delivery of £46.6m of savings proposals. While there are plans in place to deliver against these proposals there remains a risk around the timely delivery of such a large-scale programme.

findings.paper_title: Appendix 12 - Section 25 Assurance Statement 26.27
findings.headline: £1,087m debt burden, higher than typical for councils, consuming revenue resources
findings.detail: Lambeth's debt stood at £1,087m as of 31 December 2025. This debt stems from capital programmes including the Lambeth Housing Standard and the Redress scheme. The high debt level directly pressures revenue budgets through interest and MRP (minimum revenue provision). The council is now pursuing a 10-year capital strategy to minimize future borrowing.
findings.matters: High debt levels limit a council's financial flexibility and increase vulnerability to interest rate rises; lenders assess debt sustainability as a key credit metric.
findings.figures: £1,087m debt as at 31 December 2025
findings.quote: The Council continues to have a high level of debt, £1,087m as at 31 December 2025 which has a direct impact on the revenue budgets.

findings.paper_title: Appendix 12 - Section 25 Assurance Statement 26.27
findings.headline: Budget gap of £129.6m cumulatively by 2029-30 when transitional funding protection ends
findings.detail: Despite balancing 2026-27, the medium-term outlook deteriorates sharply. The MTFS projects budget gaps of £36.8m in 2027-28, £25.6m in 2028-29, rising to £67.3m in 2029-30. The cliff-edge occurs when government transitional protection expires at the end of 2028-29, exposing the council to the new Fair Funding Formula that significantly reduces its allocation.
findings.matters: A cumulative gap of this magnitude requires massive service cuts or tax increases beyond the referendum threshold; lenders need visibility of this structural funding decline.
findings.quote: There is a particular cliff-edge at the end of 2028-29 when transitional arrangements expire and the Council moves to the new Fair Funding Formula.

findings.paper_title: Appendix 12 - Section 25 Assurance Statement 26.27
findings.headline: £17.1m operational overspend in current year, driven by temporary accommodation and social care
findings.detail: Quarter 3 forecast shows the council is £17.1m overspent in 2025-26, with temporary accommodation alone £18m over budget. Additional pressures include £6.7m in Children, Families and Education and £3.7m in adult social care. A corporate contingency provision partially mitigates this, but the scale of overspend reveals structural demand pressures.
findings.matters: Operational overspends of this scale indicate the council's budget assumptions are misaligned with actual service costs; this pattern suggests future budgets may also be undeliverable.
findings.figures: £17.1m Q3 forecast overspend; temporary accommodation £18m; Children and Education £6.7m; Adult social care £3.7m
findings.quote: The Quarter 3 financial performance report shows a forecast overspend of £17.1m. The main overspending areas are on temporary accommodation which accounts for £18m of this variance with £5.6m in Growth and Environment, £6.7m Children, Families and Education and £3.7m for Integrated Health and Adult Social Care.

findings.paper_title: Appendix 12 - Section 25 Assurance Statement 26.27
findings.headline: Reserves collapsed to £5m by end of 2024-25, now a critical vulnerability
findings.detail: General reserves fell to just £5m at the end of 2024-25, almost entirely depleted by demand-driven overspending, particularly on temporary accommodation. The council is now targeting £45m (10% of net budget) through EFS. Without this rebuild, the council has minimal buffer against unexpected shocks.
findings.matters: Depleted reserves mean the council has no financial headroom to absorb demand shocks, delivery delays, or income shortfalls; this is a core risk indicator for lenders.
findings.figures: £5m general reserves end of 2024-25; target £45m (10% of net revenue budget)
findings.quote: The level of general reserves was significantly depleted due to ongoing cost pressures particularly in the costs of temporary accommodation.

findings.paper_title: Appendix 12 - Section 25 Assurance Statement 26.27
findings.headline: Council has applied for £116m government bailout to avoid insolvency
findings.detail: Lambeth cannot balance its budget without Exceptional Financial Support (EFS) funding from central government. The £116m spans 2024-25 through 2026-27 and is needed to address current overspends, rebuild depleted reserves, and fund a residual budget gap. The S151 officer describes this as a one-off request essential to reach a sustainable position.
findings.matters: A council requiring this scale of government bailout signals structural financial distress and dependency on government discretion; lenders need to know the council cannot fund itself.
findings.figures: £116m EFS application; £40m of the £116m directed to reserves rebuilding
findings.quote: This statement is made in the context of the Council's application for £116m of Exceptional Financial Support (EFS) across the period 2024-25 through to 2026-27. EFS is required to address current year issues and improve our reserves position.

findings.paper_title: Addendum to Budget Report 2026-27
findings.headline: Lambeth has been awarded Exceptional Financial Support as one of only 35 councils nationally to receive government capitalisation support
findings.detail: On 23 February 2026, Lambeth received confirmation that its application for Exceptional Financial Support was agreed in-principle. The council is one of 35 local authorities granted capitalisation support totalling £1.5bn for 2026-27, and one of eight London boroughs receiving this support. The proposed budget was drafted assuming this application would succeed, with the full cost taken into account in the MTFS.
findings.matters: EFS is emergency government support for councils in financial distress; Lambeth's budget depends entirely on this support being confirmed, indicating the council cannot balance its books without this government intervention
findings.figures: 35 local authorities, £1.5bn, 8 London boroughs, 2026-27
findings.quote: On Monday 23 February 2026, the Council received confirmation that its application for Exceptional Financial Support (EFS) has been agreed in-principle. Lambeth is one of 35 local authorities to be granted capitalisation support totalling £1.5bn for the next financial year

findings.paper_title: Budget Report 2026-27 - COUNCIL
findings.headline: Savings delivery dependent on consultation completion and income materialization with delivery risk
findings.detail: The £46.58m of agreed savings for 2026-27 includes £27.367m efficiency savings, £10.073m income generation, and £9.140m other savings that may impact service delivery. Multiple proposals are contingent on completing consultations and achieving income targets. The report notes 'risks associated with the timing of their implementation' and that delivery is 'contingent upon those income streams materialising as forecast.'
findings.matters: A lender needs confidence that savings will actually be delivered. Delays in consultation-based savings or shortfalls in income generation could widen the budget gap. The council has acknowledged these dependencies, creating execution risk.
findings.figures: Total 2026-27 savings: £46.580m (efficiency £27.367m, income £10.073m, other £9.140m); cumulative MTFS savings: £99.773m; phase 2 staffing restructure (continuing 2025-26 work of reducing directorates 7→5 and senior management -20%)
findings.quote: With regard to the proposed savings programme, there are risks associated with the timing of their implementation. Several savings proposals are dependent on the completion of consultations and subsequent decision‑making processes. Any delays to these activities will result in the reprofiling of savings

findings.paper_title: Budget Report 2026-27 - COUNCIL
findings.headline: Council Tax base declining 1.46% (1,730 band D equivalents) despite planning increases
findings.detail: Lambeth is forecasting a net tax base decrease of 1,730 band D equivalent dwellings for 2026-27 (1.46% reduction), compared to growth of 3.35% in 2025-26. The decline is attributed to overestimation of premiums on second homes and stabilization of long-term empty premiums. This is unusual for a London borough and suggests outward migration or properties leaving the tax base.
findings.matters: Declining tax base erodes council's locally-generated income and contradicts planning assumptions for financial sustainability. It reflects real economic pressures on residents (cost of living, housing costs) that are driving population movement out of the borough.
findings.figures: Tax base change: -1,730 band D equivalent dwellings (1.46% reduction vs +3.35% growth in 2025-26); council tax baseline: £173.175m; increase from tax base changes: £2.532m (negative in reality)
findings.quote: We are forecasting a net tax base decrease for 2026-27 of 1,730 band D equivalent dwellings, this represents a reduction of 1.46% (growth in 25-26 was 3.35%). This is partly due to an overestimate of the premium that is charged on second homes

findings.paper_title: Budget Report 2026-27 - COUNCIL
findings.headline: Housing Revenue Account faces £4.9bn 30-year investment backlog with aging stock
findings.detail: Lambeth is the second largest local authority landlord in London with 23,600 socially rented homes. A 2023 condition survey identified a £4.9bn investment requirement over 30 years. Most stock consists of flats averaging over 60 years old. HRA reserves were only £6.3m at March 2025 (down from higher levels), and a £40m EFS was approved for 2025-26. The HRA Recovery Plan aims to rebuild reserves to 10% of turnover (£28m) by March 2030.
findings.matters: This represents a major unfunded capital liability. The aging stock creates ongoing repair and compliance costs (disrepair claims are budgeted). HRA's financial weakness constrains the council's ability to invest in compliance and modernization, creating long-term property value and tenant satisfaction risks.
findings.figures: Housing stock: 23,600 rented homes + 10,000 leasehold properties; 30-year investment requirement: £4.9bn; HRA reserves March 2025: £6.3m (down from £12.8m decline 2022-24); EFS approved 2025-26: £40m; target reserves 2030: £28m (10% of turnover)
findings.quote: The borough's housing stock is ageing and needs investment, with most homes being flats that are on average more than 60 years old. In 2023 the Council commissioned an extensive condition survey to inform the future investment in its housing stock. This identified a £4.9bn investment requirement over the next 30 years

findings.paper_title: Budget Report 2026-27 - COUNCIL
findings.headline: Dedicated Schools Grant moving from £0.157m surplus to £12.3m deficit by 2026-27
findings.detail: The DSG is forecast to move from a small cumulative surplus of £0.157m in 2025-26 to a deficit of £12.3m by end of 2026-27. The High Needs Block deficit (£5.707m forecast for 2025-26) is driven by increasing numbers of Education Health and Care Plans (EHCPs) and rising specialist placement costs. Additionally, 22 of 64 maintained schools have licensed deficits totalling £12.2m for 2025-26, an increase of £1m from 2024-25.
findings.matters: The DSG deficit reflects cost pressures in SEND provision that are unfunded. While currently ringfenced from General Fund via statutory override (to 2027-28), this creates a latent liability. School deficits also pose risk: if maintained schools with deficits convert to academies, those deficits transfer to the General Fund.
findings.figures: DSG cumulative position: £0.157m surplus (2025-26) → £12.3m deficit (2026-27); High Needs Block deficit £5.707m (2025-26) and £5.707m forecast cumulative; maintained school licensed deficits: £12.2m (2025-26), up from £11.2m (2024-25)
findings.quote: Based on the proposed budgets, the DSG is expected to move from the current small surplus position, to close 2026-27 with an overall cumulative deficit of £12.3m. This is driven by the High Needs Block forecast deficit, which reflects both increasing numbers of Education Health and Care Plans (EHCPs) and the rising cost of specialist placements, particularly for pupils with complex needs.

findings.paper_title: Budget Report 2026-27 - COUNCIL
findings.headline: Funding allocation reduced £17.5m under Fair Funding Review 2.0, with inner London boroughs facing 15.5% average cuts
findings.detail: The Fair Funding Review 2.0 (FFR2.0) fundamentally reset funding shares. Lambeth's allocation fell £17.5m compared to 2025-26 even after accounting for rolled-in grants. Inner London boroughs like Lambeth face average reductions of 15.5% over three years (2026-29), while outer London boroughs see increases of 31.5%. This creates a two-tier system within the same region.
findings.matters: The government funding reform has reduced Lambeth's long-term baseline. The council faces structural underfunding compared to outer London peers. The recovery grant and 100% income protection are temporary (ending after 2028-29), meaning the full impact of the reduction will be felt in 2029-30.
findings.figures: Funding allocation reduction: £17.5m; inner London average reduction: 15.5% over 2026-29; outer London average increase: 31.5%; recovery grant (temporary): 5% in 2026-27, 6% by 2027-28, 7% by 2028-29 with £35m cap
findings.quote: This variation is also seen in the difference between outer and inner London boroughs, with outer London boroughs seeing average increases of 31.5% in Fair Funding Allocation but inner London boroughs like Lambeth with average reductions of 15.5% over the three years.

findings.paper_title: Budget Report 2026-27 - COUNCIL
findings.headline: General Fund reserves depleted to £5m and dependent on EFS to recover to prudent level
findings.detail: General Fund reserves fell to £5m at March 2025 after reductions of £12.8m (2022-23), £12.5m (2023-24), and £8.6m (2024-25). The S151 officer states the council should maintain reserves at 10% of net revenue expenditure (c£45m). EFS provides £40m specifically to rebuild reserves to this level. External auditors raised statutory recommendations about reserve adequacy in February 2025.
findings.matters: Depleted reserves mean the council has minimal buffer against unexpected shocks or demand fluctuations. The audit concerns signal external validation that the council's financial resilience is inadequate for a local authority of this size.
findings.figures: Reserves at March 2025: £5m; target: £45m (10% of £471.852m net revenue); EFS provision for reserve rebuild: £40m
findings.quote: It is the view of the S151 officer that the council should maintain reserves at 10% or net revenue expenditure (c£45m). This is set out in the council's Reserves Strategy at Appendix 11. This also responds directly to concerns raised by the External Auditor in their statutory recommendations issued in February 2025.

findings.paper_title: Budget Report 2026-27 - COUNCIL
findings.headline: Structural budget deficits of £129.6m cumulative by 2029-30 despite £46.58m annual savings
findings.detail: Even after delivering £46.58m of agreed savings in 2026-27, the council faces budget gaps of £36.76m (2027-28), £25.56m (2028-28), and £67.28m (2029-30). The cumulative shortfall over four years is £129.6m. The report notes that funding 'will take years to make up for the real terms reduction in funding experienced for well over a decade' and that 'a permanently reduced financial envelope' is expected.
findings.matters: The council cannot close the budget gap through savings delivery alone. There is no realistic plan to address the £129.6m cumulative shortfall, suggesting further EFS applications or service cuts will be necessary.
findings.quote: Bringing together our assumptions on funding and expenditure over the next three years, we see budget shortfalls in every year from 2027-28 to 2029-30.

findings.paper_title: Budget Report 2026-27 - COUNCIL
findings.headline: Temporary accommodation spending reaches £105m annually with unfunded shortfall growing
findings.detail: Lambeth spent £100m on temporary accommodation in 2024-25, with spend forecast at £105m in 2025-26 and projected to reduce to £90m in 2026-27 through new initiatives. However, Housing Benefit income covers less than 40% of costs (£40m of £100m spend), leaving a structural funding gap. London boroughs collectively spend £5m per day on temporary accommodation. The issue is recognized as 'unsustainable, both locally and nationally.'
findings.matters: This represents a massive, growing unfunded liability driven by housing policy and demographics outside the council's control. It is the single largest driver of London boroughs' financial pressures and continues to destabilize the council's budget.
findings.figures: £100m+ spend in 2024-25; £105m forecast for 2025-26; £90m planned for 2026-27; income only £40m (40% coverage); 30% increase in expenditure 2023-24 (16% volume increase × 14% rate increase); London boroughs spending £5m daily
findings.quote: Temporary accommodation income from Housing Benefit and rents is based on 2011 Local Housing Allowance and so has not kept pace with the growth in expenditure over the past 13 years. Income from TA rents funds less than 40% of the cost of the accommodation.

findings.paper_title: Budget Report 2026-27 - COUNCIL
findings.headline: Budget cannot be balanced without £20m Exceptional Financial Support in 2026-27
findings.detail: The council is applying for £116m of EFS across 2024-25 to 2026-27, with £20m specifically needed to balance the 2026-27 budget. This is on top of £40m already approved for the HRA in 2025-26. The report states this is 'a one-off measure' but EFS is essentially government-backed borrowing to fund day-to-day services, not investment.
findings.matters: A lender would want to know the council cannot balance its day-to-day budget from its own resources and is dependent on government emergency support to avoid insolvency.
findings.figures: £116m EFS application (2024-25 to 2026-27), of which £20m is for 2026-27 budget gap; £40m for General Fund reserves rebuild; £16m for bad debt provisions; £40m for underlying overspend and one-off pressures
findings.quote: it is estimated, over £130m of further proposals will need to be found over the next four years. Change on this scale will take time and so we will be using Exceptional Financial Support from the Government to balance the budget for 2026-27 which we are assuming will be agreed.

findings.paper_title: HRA Rent and Service Charge Setting Report
findings.headline: Building and fire safety regulations impose unfunded compliance costs on top of existing budget pressures
findings.detail: Post-Grenfell fire safety programme is underway (100% compliance achieved). New housing regulations from 2026 onwards add additional requirements for damp, excess cold, falls, structural collapse, electrical hazards, and others. Paper explicitly states 'costs arising from enhanced Fire Safety have not been fully met by central Government funding.'
findings.matters: Unfunded regulatory compliance adds unbudgeted cost pressures to already constrained HRA, limiting discretionary spending
findings.figures: 100% Fire Risk Assessment compliance; new regulations phased 2026-2027; multiple hazard categories added
findings.quote: Maintaining Fire Safety is a shared obligation between residents and the Council and costs arising from enhanced Fire Safety have not been fully met by central Government funding.

findings.paper_title: HRA Rent and Service Charge Setting Report
findings.headline: Housing stock averaging 60+ years old requires £4.9bn investment over 30 years against £61m annual capital budget
findings.detail: 2023 condition survey identified £4.9bn investment need over 30 years to maintain and upgrade housing, including carbon net-zero measures. Current capital programme budgeted at £61m annually, insufficient to meet identified need. Most homes are flats predating 1965.
findings.matters: Underfunded capital maintenance on aging stock creates long-term deterioration risk, compliance exposure, and eventual need for major reinvestment
findings.figures: £4.9bn required over 30 years; £61m annual capital budget; average property age 60+ years
findings.quote: The borough's housing is ageing and needs investment, with most homes being flats that are on average more than 60 years old...This identified a £4.9bn investment requirement over the next 30 years, including Lambeth's wider efforts to move towards its carbon net zero ambitions.

findings.paper_title: HRA Rent and Service Charge Setting Report
findings.headline: Bad debt provision increasing due to cost-of-living crisis with 37% of tenants unsubsidised by benefits
findings.detail: Council notes 'The % of bad debts has increased in recent years' reflecting the cost-of-living crisis. Of 22,466 tenanted properties, 8,351 (37%) receive no Housing Benefit or Universal Credit, making them liable for full rent and service charges — creating collection risk during economic stress.
findings.matters: Rising arrears indicate deteriorating tenant affordability and collection risk, requiring larger bad debt provisions
findings.figures: 37% of tenants (8,351) without benefit coverage; 8% partial Housing Benefit; 38% Universal Credit claimants; 17% full Housing Benefit
findings.quote: Bad and doubtful debts – this is a provision for the non-payment of rent and service charges. The % of bad debts has increased in recent years and takes account of the impact of the cost-of-living crisis and the ability to recover debt.

findings.paper_title: HRA Rent and Service Charge Setting Report
findings.headline: HRA borrowing increasing to £15m+ annually with compounding interest costs and £2m annual debt repayment charge
findings.detail: Borrowing increased from £14m (2024/25) to £15m (2025/26), adding £1.5m in interest costs. EFS-related borrowing adds £2m interest charge. Council must also repay the £40m EFS capitalisation over 20 years via £2m annual MRP (Minimum Revenue Provision) charge — a debt service obligation that persists regardless of budget performance.
findings.matters: Growing debt service obligations (£4m+ annually) constrain future spending flexibility and must be serviced before discretionary spending
findings.figures: £14m borrowing 2024/25; £15m projected 2025/26; £1.5m additional interest; £2m EFS interest charge; £2m annual MRP
findings.quote: In 2024/25 the HRA was required to borrow £14m and projected to borrowing £15m in 2025/26, this will result in an increase of £1.5m. In addition, the borrowing relating to the £40m EFS would result in a £2m interest charge.

findings.paper_title: HRA Rent and Service Charge Setting Report
findings.headline: Council required £40m Exceptional Financial Support capitalisation directive due to high volume of disrepair claims
findings.detail: The council applied for and received emergency government support specifically for housing disrepair liability. While the capitalisation directive relieves immediate cash pressure, it 'does not provide additional resource to fund the cost pressure or the repayment of debt.' The council has £13.7m of assets in sale progression to repay this borrowing.
findings.matters: Material unresolved housing disrepair liability required emergency government support and will require asset sales to repay
findings.figures: £40m capitalisation directive; £13.7m of assets progressed for sale
findings.quote: Due to these unprecedented pressures and a high volume of disrepair cases causing a substantial liability, the Council applied for Exception Financial Support from Ministry for Housing, Communities and Local Government (MHCLG).

findings.paper_title: HRA Rent and Service Charge Setting Report
findings.headline: Government rent policies have created a permanent £1bn+ structural deficit over 30 years, limiting investment in housing stock
findings.detail: Rent reduction policy 2016-2020 cost £37.2m cumulatively; 7% rent cap in 2023 created additional losses. These two policy decisions alone created a shortfall of over £1bn over the 30-year business plan period. Rent convergence to recover the gap will take up to 15 years, creating a long-term structural constraint on investment.
findings.matters: A £1bn structural deficit is a permanent reduction in HRA's ability to fund the £4.9bn housing stock condition needs and limits financial flexibility
findings.figures: £37.2m cumulative loss 2016-2020; over £1bn total 30-year shortfall; 15 years to recover convergence gap
findings.quote: These two decisions alone have left the HRA with a shortfall of over £1bn over the course of the 30-year HRA business plan period, reducing the resources available to reinvest in our housing stock.

findings.paper_title: HRA Rent and Service Charge Setting Report
findings.headline: HRA reserves depleted to £5.7m from £39.6m in four years, with critical shortfall against recommended £20m minimum
findings.detail: Reserves fell from £39.6m in April 2022 to £5.7m by April 2025, a 86% reduction driven by accumulated deficits. Paper forecasts recovery to £15.1m by March 2026, but acknowledges this remains far short of the 10% of turnover minimum (£20m). The depletion rate has slowed but the reserve position is described as concerning.
findings.matters: Depleted reserves reduce financial resilience for unforeseen shocks and indicate structural pressures in the core budget
findings.figures: April 2022: £39.6m; April 2023: £26.8m; April 2024: £14.4m; April 2025: £5.7m; forecast March 2026: £15.1m
findings.quote: The level of reserves is concerning and replenishing reserves to a minimum level of £20m needs to be a key priority.

findings.paper_title: HRA Rent and Service Charge Setting Report
findings.headline: External auditors have issued statutory recommendations expressing concern about the council's ability to balance budget and maintain reserves
findings.detail: The council's auditors have formally flagged concerns about HRA financial sustainability. This moves beyond routine audit commentary to statutory recommendations — a signal that the audit process has identified material risks to financial viability that management must address.
findings.matters: Statutory audit recommendations indicate compliance risk and auditor doubt about management's ability to deliver on stated financial plans
findings.figures: Statutory recommendations on budget and reserves management
findings.quote: The Council's external auditors have issued statutory recommendations expressing concern about the Council's ability to balance its budget and reserves levels.
